# The MR Macroscopic Model

{{< include "includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The standard MR macroscopic model

```{=html}
<!--
![The standard MR macroscopic model.](images/ch06/the-standard-mr-macroscopic-model.png){#fig-ch06-the-standard-mr-macroscopic-model}
-->
```

The free-induction-decay (FID) signal is produced by the net magnetization of hydrogen nuclei, primarily those in water. Each hydrogen nucleus is a proton with spin and an associated magnetic moment. This chapter introduces the macroscopic model that describes how the static field and RF excitation produce a measurable MR signal.

## The MR signal arises from hydrogen nuclei (spins, protons)

![Source of the MR signal: Hydrogen nuclei (spins, protons) (after Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 3.2).](images/ch06/source-of-the-mr-signal-hydrogen-nuclei-spins-prot.png){#fig-ch06-source-of-the-mr-signal-hydrogen-nuclei-spins-prot}

Although spin is a quantum-mechanical property, it is useful to represent a proton as a small magnetic dipole. The classical picture in @fig-ch06-nucleus-spin depicts this dipole precessing about the main magnetic field, $B_0$; it should not be interpreted as a literal spinning charged sphere.

![A simplified classical depiction of a proton magnetic moment precessing about the main field, $B_0$.](images/ch06/nucleus-spin.png){#fig-ch06-nucleus-spin}

In the absence of an applied field, an ensemble of proton magnetic moments has no preferred direction, so its net magnetization is zero. Placing the sample in $B_0$ establishes a preferred longitudinal direction. An RF field, $B_1$, applied near the Larmor frequency can then rotate the bulk magnetization away from that direction.

![A simplified classical depiction of a magnetic moment precessing about $B_0$.](images/ch06/nucleus-precession.png){#fig-ch06-nucleus-precession width="20%"}

Precession is analogous to the motion of a spinning top in Earth's gravitational field: the direction of the magnetic moment traces a cone around the $z$-axis. For a single spin-$1/2$ proton, a measurement of the spin component along $B_0$ has one of two values, conventionally called parallel and antiparallel. In an ensemble at thermal equilibrium, there is a small excess in the lower-energy, parallel state. That excess produces the longitudinal equilibrium magnetization, $M_0$, illustrated in @fig-ch06-nuclei-aligned.

![A schematic ensemble of proton magnetic moments without an applied field (left) and in the main field, $B_0$ (right). The small population excess parallel to $B_0$ produces a net magnetization, $M_0$.](images/ch06/nuclei-aligned.png){#fig-ch06-nuclei-aligned}

::: {.callout-note title="Drawing single NMR spins"}
*Drawing single NMR spins and understanding relaxation, Mike P. Williamson, Sheffield*

"How should we draw vectors to represent individual nuclear spins? Vectors in 3D space are merely a way of understanding the mathematics of quantum mechanics, which provides the “true” description of a single spin-½ nucleus. They are a useful aid to understanding, but there is no single “correct” vector representation, and the different vector models that are used have advantages and disadvantages. Here, we discuss the 2 standard vector models for a nuclear magnetic resonance spin: the up/down or alignment model and the 2-cone model, and we show how they relate to quantum mechanics. We show why both of these models are limited and discuss a third model, the uniform model, in which individual spins can be in any orientation. We demonstrate how the uniform model presents a clear and logically coherent description for spins: at equilibrium; following a 90° pulse; and during the subsequent relaxation back to equilibrium. The uniform model is fully consistent with quantum mechanics and leads to an understanding of coherence and relaxation that cannot be obtained from the other 2 models. We suggest that the uniform model is more helpful than the other 2 for most purposes."
:::

## The FID signal:  Relaxation

![The FID signal (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 3.5).](images/ch06/the-fid-signal-quantal-description.png){#fig-ch06-the-fid-signal-quantal-description}

**It is very important to understand this point**

After an RF excitation pulse, the distribution of spins is changed from its steady-state condition. The physical mechanisms responsible for their return to the steady-state - this return is called **relaxation** - differs between the z-axis and the x-y plane. We use a different model for these two types of relaxation.

## The net magnetization is the sum of the spins

![The net magnetization is the sum of the spins (after Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 3.7).](images/ch06/the-net-magnetization-is-the-sum-of-the-spins.png){#fig-ch06-the-net-magnetization-is-the-sum-of-the-spins}

We summarize the behavior of the spins by calculating the **net magnetization**, which is the vector sum of all the individual spins. The net magnetization vector ($\mathbf{M}$) points in the direction of the majority of the spins and has a magnitude proportional to the number of spins aligned in that direction. At equilibrium, the net magnetization points along the direction of the $B_0$ field (the $z$-axis) because more spins are aligned with $B_0$ than against it.

## Applying the RF field tips the net magnetization

![The RF field tips the net magnetization.](images/ch06/applying-the-rf-field-rotates-all-the-spins.png){#fig-ch06-applying-the-rf-field-rotates-all-the-spins}

## The $B_1$ field creates transverse magnetization

```{=html}
<!--
![The $B_1$ field applies a torque that creates transverse magnetization.](images/ch06/the-b1-signal-applies-a-force-to-the-net-magnetiza.png){#fig-ch06-the-b1-signal-applies-a-force-to-the-net-magnetiza}
-->
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![The $B_1$ field applies a torque that tips $\mathbf{M}$ away from the $z$-axis, creating transverse magnetization.](images/ch06/b1-force-creates-transverse-signal.mp4){#vid-ch06-b1-force-creates-transverse-signal width="70%" loop="true" autoplay="true" muted="true"}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
![The $B_1$ field applies a torque that tips $\mathbf{M}$ away from the $z$-axis, creating transverse magnetization (video; see the HTML version for the animation).](images/ch06/b1-force-creates-transverse-signal.png){width="70%"}
:::

-   The RF field produced by the transmit coil, $B_1$, applies a torque that tips the net magnetization, $\mathbf{M}$, away from the $z$-axis.
-   After excitation, the transverse magnetization, $M_{xy}$, precesses about the main field, $B_0$.

In the usual idealized description, the RF field is transverse to $B_0$ and oscillates near the Larmor frequency. Its transverse components, $B_{1x}$ and $B_{1y}$, efficiently tip $\mathbf{M}$ and create $M_{xy}$. A field component parallel to $B_0$, $B_{1z}$, produces no torque on magnetization already aligned with $B_0$ and therefore does not directly produce transverse magnetization. RF coils are designed to generate the intended transverse $B_1$ field as uniformly as practical across the region of interest.

## Measuring the net magnetization

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![The precessing net magnetization induces a signal in a receiver coil (shown here as the copper coil), which can be the same as or different from the transmit coil.](images/ch06/measuring-net-magnetization-coil.mp4){#vid-ch06-measuring-net-magnetization-coil width="70%" loop="true" autoplay="true" muted="true"}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
![The precessing net magnetization induces a signal in a receiver coil (video; see the HTML version for the animation).](images/ch06/measuring-net-magnetization-coil.png){width="70%"}
:::

-   The precessing transverse magnetization produces a changing magnetic flux through the receiver coil.
-   The changing flux induces the measured voltage signal in the receiver coil.
-   The receiver coil (shown here as the copper coil) can be the same as, or separate from, the RF transmit coil.

## The RF field ($B_1$)

![The RF field, $B_1$, in the rotating-frame and laboratory-frame views (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e).](images/ch06/the-rf-signal-b1-causes-the-net-magnetization-to-p.png){#fig-ch06-the-rf-signal-b1-causes-the-net-magnetization-to-p}

## The receive coil measures an induced voltage

![The receive coil measures the electrical radio frequency signal from the spins — step 2 (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 3.16).](images/ch06/the-receive-coil-measures-the-electrical-radio-fre-2.png){#fig-ch06-the-receive-coil-measures-the-electrical-radio-fre-2}

As the transverse net magnetization precesses about the $z$-axis, the magnetic flux through the receiver coil changes. By Faraday's law, this changing flux induces a voltage whose sign and magnitude vary over time. The receiver records this voltage as the MR signal.

The signal requires phase coherence among spins in the transverse ($x$-$y$) plane, which produces a nonzero transverse net magnetization.

## Explaining the FID signal dependence on B1 duration

![From earlier: The FID signal depends on the B1 duration.](images/ch06/remember-the-fid-signal-depends-on-the-b1-duration.png){#fig-ch06-remember-the-fid-signal-depends-on-the-b1-duration}

Because the spins are rotated, the signal increases up to the 90 deg rotation when the spins are fully in the transverse (x-y) plane; the signal starts to decrease as the rotation moves the net magnetization to 180 deg where it has no (x-y) component. This explains the increase and decrease in @fig-ch06-remember-the-fid-signal-depends-on-the-b1-duration.

The amount of rotation due to the RF pulse, measured as an angle, is called the **flip angle**.

![Applying the RF field rotates the spins, rotating the net magnetization.](images/ch06/applying-the-rf-field-rotates-all-the-spins.png)

The longer duration (or higher amplitude) of the B1 pulse increses the amount of rotation. This explains why the FID signal increases with the increasing duration (or amplitude) of the RF excitation, but up to a point.  When the flip angle is 90 degrees, that's as big as the transverse signal will get.  Beyond that it gets smaller and returns to zero at a 180 deg flip angle.  If you keep going, the signal will return.
